title: Life histories: fast or slow?
sub: Symposium topic 1 · Stearns 1977 vs Stott et al. 2024
blurb: Life-history traits, the slow–fast continuum, pace-of-life syndromes and why one axis is not enough.
h1: Does the fast–slow continuum capture life-history variation?
lede: Group 1's question: does the fast–slow continuum capture life-history variation across taxa, or do we need several axes? Classic paper Stearns (1977), recent paper Stott et al. (2024), 'Life histories are not just fast or slow'.
six: **Life-history traits**: growth, age and size at maturity, number and size of offspring, lifespan.
**Fast** = early reproduction, many small offspring, short life, high mortality. **Slow** = the opposite.
The **slow–fast continuum** is the main axis, defined by the trade-off between time spent on reproduction and development versus survival.
**Pace-of-life syndromes** add behaviour and physiology: fast, bold, high-metabolism vs slow, shy, low-metabolism.
It works as the dominant axis in tetrapods, and broadly in vascular plants and corals; few studies in invertebrates (except insects).
Answer: the fast–slow axis is the main one for some taxa, but **multiple axes** are needed (e.g. reproductive patterns, stature–recruitment, altricial vs precocial).
foot: Source: Group 1 symposium slides; glossary section 2; Stearns 1977; Stott et al. 2024.

questions.q: Which of these is a life-history trait?
questions.e: Life-history traits concern growth, reproduction and survival: age at maturity, offspring number and size, lifespan.

questions.q: Which set describes a FAST life history?
questions.answer: Early reproduction, many small offspring, short lifespan
wrong: Late reproduction, few large offspring, long lifespan
Early reproduction, few large offspring, long lifespan
Late reproduction, many small offspring, short lifespan
questions.e: Fast = early, many, small, short-lived, high mortality.

questions.q: Group 1's example of a fast species, with a 10–12 day life cycle, is…
questions.e: Drosophila melanogaster: 10–12 days at room temperature.

questions.q: Group 1's slow example, mature at 4–5 years and living about 20 years, is…
questions.e: Slow: later maturation, fewer offspring, longer life.

questions.q: The slow–fast continuum is defined by the trade-off between…
questions.answer: Time for reproduction and development versus survival
questions.e: Group 1: an axis defined by allocating time to reproduction and development versus survival.

questions.q: Pace-of-life syndromes add which kinds of traits to life history?
questions.e: E.g. fast-growing, bold, high-metabolism vs slow-growing, shy, low-metabolism.

questions.q: Where does the fast–slow axis work best as the dominant axis, per Group 1?
questions.e: Broad picture in tetrapods; also vascular plants and corals; few studies in invertebrates except insects.

questions.q: What was Group 1's answer to the guiding question?
questions.answer: Fast–slow is the main axis for some taxa, but multiple axes are needed
questions.e: Many organisms fall outside fast–slow predictions.

questions.q: The kapok tree (low recruitment) vs Psychotria horizontalis (high recruitment) illustrate which extra axis?
questions.e: Recruitment = rate of adding new individuals to a population segment.

questions.q: Young that are born helpless and need care are called…
questions.e: Group 1 contrasted altricial and precocial offspring as another axis.

questions.q: Sockeye salmon vs European rabbit was Group 1's example for which trait?
questions.answer: Parity (how many times an organism breeds)
questions.e: Parity is a life-history trait: the salmon breeds once, the rabbit many times.

questions.q: Which recent paper did Group 1 use?
questions.answer: Stott et al. 2024, Life histories are not just fast or slow
